Group 6 - Acute coronary syndrome and Africa

Studio wall

Author

Kasyap N R, Rachana, Jayani (Panels A & B); Kasyap N R, Madhumitha, Jai, Jayani (Panel C)

Spine

Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where in Africa is life short?

This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it. If a plot cannot be introduced in a clause that hangs off this line, it is off the wall.

Introduction - the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Four tables, four shapes.

  • Panel A (panel-A.csv) - ACS clinic file: age, height, weight, BMI, ejection fraction, lipids. sex and obesity for grouping.
  • Panel B (panel-B.csv) - same people, categorical information.
  • Panel C (panel-C.csv) - Africa data.
  • Panel D (panel-D.csv) - selected Hinkley monitoring well chromium data.

We load from this folder:

2. Ask

Questions this table can answer. 1. Is age associated with EF? 2. Is TC associated with LDLC? 3. Does EF differ between males and females? 4. Does obesity status vary between males and females? 5. Is obesity independent of age? 6. Does height, age and sex of the person effect BMI? 7. Does EF decrease with age? 8. Does the proportion of obese and non obese patients differ between males and females? 9. Do obese patients generally show higher BMI values than non-obese patients? 10.How many obese and non-obese participants are there in the dataset? 11.How are the participants’ weights distributed? 12.What is the age distribution of the participants?

One question this table cannot answer. 1. Is regular physical activity associated with ejection fraction (EF)? 2. Does smoking cause higher cholesterol? 3. Do diabetic patients have higher BMI? 4. Does high blood pressure lead to lower EF? 5. Does obesity cause a lower ejection fraction? 6. Which patients had a STEMI, NSTEMI, or Unstable Angina? 7. Will patients with high BMI develop heart disease in the future?

3. Choose a mark

Use bar charts, histograms, box plots, or scatter plots depending on the type of variables and the questions being answered.

4. Predict

I expect some variables such as BMI and obesity status to show clear differences, while relationships involving age, EF.

5. Make

Create the graphs using ggplot2, and summaries or statistical tests where appropriate to examine the pattern in the data.

6. Say

  1. Does height, age and sex of the person effect BMI? Ans. This graph is special because height and BMI are shown through position, while sex is shown by color and age by the size of the points.

7. Limit

Panel A can only answer questions using the variables available in the table. It cannot answer questions about smoking, diagnosis, diabetes etc..

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. 1.Does smoking status vary by sex? 2.Are the observed obesity patterns for males and females different from what would be expected by chance? 3.Does smoking status differ across STEMI, NSTEMI, and Unstable Angina patients? 4.Is obesity distributed differently across the different diagnosis groups? 5.Is cardiogenic shock more common in certain diagnosis groups? 6.Does the type of entry, Radial or Femoral, differ across diagnosis groups? 7.Is diabetes associated with high blood pressure? 8.Is cardiogenic shock associated with smoking status?

One question this table cannot answer. 1. What is the average age of patients with STEMI? Ans. Age is not available in Panel B.

  1. Do obese patients have a higher BMI than non-obese patients? Ans. BMI values are not available in Panel B.

  2. Do smokers have higher cholesterol levels than non-smokers? Ans. Cholestrol levels are not available in Panel B.

  3. Do patients with diabetes have a lower ejection fraction? Ans. Ejection fraction is not available in Panel B.

  4. Which patients recovered faster after treatment? Ans. Panel B does not contain treatment or recovery time information.

  5. How long had each patient been smoking? Ans. Panel B gives smoking status but not the duration of smoking.

3. Choose a mark

Use bar chart and mosaic plots to compare qualitative variables, followed by chi-square test.

4. Predict

I expect some qualitative variables to show clear differences between groups, while others may show little or no difference.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. 1. Which countries have the lowest life expectancy? 2. Is there a relation between population of a country and GDP per capita? Is GDP per capita higher with higher population?

One question this table cannot answer.

  1. Why do some countries have a high GDP per capita but low life expectancy?
  2. What percentage of women help a country build its GDP per capita?

3. Choose a mark

Question 1: Which countries have the lowest life expectancy?

Mark: A map of Africa where countries are filled based on life expectancy.

Question 2: Is there a relation between population of a country and GDP per capita? Is GDP per capita higher with higher population?

Mark:A map of Africa showing GDP per capita using fill colour and population using border colour.

4. Predict

We expect life expectancy to vary across African countries. We also expect population and GDP per capita to show some relationship, but it may not be very strong.

5. Make

C_modd |>
  ggformula::gf_sf(
    geometry = ~geometry,
    fill = ~lifeExp,
    color = "black"
  )
C_modd |>
  ggformula::gf_sf(
    geometry = ~geometry,
    fill = ~gdpPercap,
    color = ~pop
  ) |>
  ggformula::gf_refine(
    ggplot2::scale_color_gradient(
      low = "#A1FA4F",
      high = "#183E0C"
    )
  ) |>
  ggformula::gf_refine(
    ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(
      low = "#FFFE91",
      high = "#BA1B1B"
    )
  )

6. Say

Title: Africa: A Data Visualization

Caption: These maps show differences in life expectancy, population and GDP per capita across African countries.

One statement we will stand by: The data shows clear differences in life expectancy, population and GDP per capita across African countries

7. Limit

This panel only contains data from 2007, so we cannot study how these values changed over time. It also does not contain gender data, so we cannot compare life expectancy or GDP per capita between women and men.

2. Ask

Questions this table can answer.

  1. Which selected monitoring well has the highest and lowest Cr(VI) concentration?
  2. How do Cr(VI) and Cr(T) concentrations compare across the selected monitoring wells?

Questions this table cannot answer.

  1. Why do chromium concentrations differ between the monitoring wells?
  2. Did the chromium contamination cause health problems for people living in Hinkley?

3. Choose a mark

Question 1: Which selected monitoring well has the highest and lowest Cr(VI) concentration?

Mark: A bar chart comparing Cr(VI) concentration across the selected monitoring wells.

Question 2: How do Cr(VI) and Cr(T) concentrations compare across the selected monitoring wells?

Mark: A grouped bar chart comparing Cr(VI) and Cr(T) concentrations for each selected monitoring well.

4. Predict

We expect Cr(VI) concentrations to differ across the selected monitoring wells. We also expect Cr(T) values to be similar to, or slightly higher than, Cr(VI) at most wells.

5. Make

Question 1: Which selected monitoring well has the highest and lowest Cr(VI) concentration?

ggplot2::ggplot(D, ggplot2::aes(x = well, y = CrVI)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col()

Question 2: How do Cr(VI) and Cr(T) concentrations compare across the selected monitoring wells?

D_long <- D |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(CrVI, CrT),
    names_to = "chromium_type",
    values_to = "concentration"
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(
  D_long,
  ggplot2::aes(
    x = well,
    y = concentration,
    fill = chromium_type
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(position = "dodge")

6. Say

Title: Chromium levels across selected Hinkley monitoring wells

Caption: These graphs compare Cr(VI) and total dissolved chromium, Cr(T), across seven selected monitoring wells from the Second Quarter 2026 Hinkley plume map.

One statement we will stand by: Chromium concentrations differ across the selected wells, and Cr(T) is equal to or slightly higher than Cr(VI) at most of the wells.

7. Limit

This panel uses only seven selected monitoring wells from one part of the Second Quarter 2026 plume map. It does not represent every well in Hinkley, and it cannot explain why chromium levels differ between wells or what health effects they may have caused.

Conclusion

What the spine looks like after four panels.

The question we will defend in ninety seconds:
What patterns can we find from the health data, differences between African countries, and chromium levels in selected Hinkley monitoring wells?

What we will not claim: We will not say that one variable is causing another just because we found a relationship between them.

Which lines were human, which were machine: Most of the questions and observations were discussed by us. AI was used in some places to help us understand the code, fix errors and organise the work.

Limits:
All the panels do not contain the same variables, so some questions cannot be answered. Panel C also contains data only from 2007, so we cannot understand changes over time. Panel D uses only seven selected monitoring wells, so it does not represent all wells in Hinkley.

Gift for the steal-this strip:
Joining the country names in Panel C with the world map data and using the geometry column to show the values on a map.
